query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a tungsten-rich or silicide-based refractory coating on steel rollers and guide plates used in hot-dip aluminum plating lines will significantly reduce molten aluminum corrosion and extend their service life by at least a factor of two compared to uncoated steels.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional steel rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates used in high-temperature hot-dip aluminum plating operations.
generation.intervention: Apply a dense, adherent tungsten-rich or silicide-based layer via pack cementation or advanced cladding methods to form a stable diffusion barrier on the steel surfaces.
generation.conditions: Continuous immersion and contact with high-temperature molten aluminum in industrial plating lines over prolonged service cycles.
generation.structural_mediator: A refractory surface layer that isolates the steel substrate from direct chemical attack by molten aluminum.
generation.mechanism: The refractory-based coating resists dissolution and oxidation by forming a stable barrier, limiting Al infiltration and reducing corrosive wear on the underlying steel substrate.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated components experience substantially less corrosive degradation and attain a service life at least twice that of uncoated steels under the same high-temperature molten aluminum exposure.
generation.baseline: Uncoated steel equipment components suffer from severe and rapid erosion under long-term exposure to molten aluminum, significantly shortening component lifespan.
generation.boundary: Performance depends on coating composition, thickness, and integrity as well as service conditions such as temperature, immersion time, and chemical composition of the molten aluminum bath.
generation.uncertainty: Exact lifespan improvements and optimal coating compositions may vary with process parameters, and further testing is required to quantify performance in different operational conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Expose coated vs. uncoated steel coupons to molten aluminum at typical hot-dip plating temperatures for extended periods. Periodically compare mass changes, perform metallographic examinations, and measure thickness loss or microstructural degradation across duplicate test samples.
measurements: Mass loss or gain of coupons
Change in coating thickness and adherence (via cross-sectional microscopy)
Chemical composition changes at the steel-coating-Al interfaces (via EDS or other standard methods)
Extent of surface damage and mechanical property retention of the coupons
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If coated samples do not demonstrate substantially reduced corrosion rates or if their service life is not measurably improved relative to the uncoated baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. The research shows that adding the proper amount of Al, Cr, and Si elements into the refractory high-entropy alloy can form a dense oxidation film on the surface of the alloy in a high-temperature environment, thus improving the high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] ]. Refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEA, also called multi‐principal‐element refractory alloys) comprise five or more principal elements from the refractory transition metals (group 4–6 elements: Zr, Hf, V, Nb, Ta, Mo, and W, often with Ti and Cr also considered), [ [1] , [2] , [3] ] with structural applications under extreme temperature conditions, beyond those where nickel‐based superalloys can be used. [ [4] ] Additive manufacturing (AM) of RHEAs can facilitate the exploration of possible applications for RHEA via rapid prototyping of parts with complex shapes with high powder feedstock utilization. Recently, laser melting deposition (LMD) was used to fabricate NbTaTiZr, [ [5] ] HfNbTiZr, [ [6] ] HfNbTaTiZr, [ [7] , [8] ] and MoNbTaW [ [9] , [10] , [11] ] quaternary and quinary refractory concentrated alloys. However, the feature resolution of LMD is relatively low, as the size of the melt pool is as large as ≈3 mm. [ [7] , [8] ] In addition, no complex parts have been demonstrated for these refractory alloys by using LMD. decision.trend: Several studies on refractory high-entropy alloys and coatings address operation in extreme environments where materials must resist high-temperature corrosion or oxidation. In PMC6908586, a CrMnFeNi HEA was tested in a molten salt environment (FLiBe), demonstrating the challenges of handling ongoing corrosion and elemental dissolution in high-temperature liquid media. In PMC10142552, a tungsten-rich multi-principal-element coating (WVTaTiCr) was developed by laser cladding, illustrating how refractory metals with tailored microstructures can enhance mechanical strength and oxidation resistance at elevated temperatures. In PMC11077685, a silicide surface treatment improved oxidation resistance for HfNbTaTiZr refractory alloys, highlighting the effectiveness of surface engineering to protect against aggressive environments. Although these papers do not directly address liquid aluminum, the same fundamental challenge of prolonged exposure to a reactive high-temperature liquid remains unsolved. The need is for a material solution that stabilizes component surfaces against molten aluminum’s severe corrosive attack.
decision.unsolved: Demonstrating a protective material or coating against molten aluminum remains an open challenge. While advanced refractory high-entropy alloys and protective coatings show promise for general high-temperature corrosion environments (oxidation and molten salts), there is a lack of direct, systematic exploration of methods to control or prevent dissolution in molten aluminum, which is known to be especially reactive with most metals.
decision.lever: Deposit a refractory-based protective coating (e.g., tungsten-rich or silicide-based) onto steel roll and guide components, with controlled thickness and dense, adherent microstructure via pack cementation or advanced cladding methods that can form a stable diffusion barrier against molten aluminum.
decision.why: Building on the success of refractory high-entropy alloy coatings and silicide diffusion layers in harsh environments, a tailored surface-engineered layer can provide chemical stability and enhanced mechanical durability in direct contact with hot aluminum. This approach specifically addresses molten aluminum’s aggressive corrosion, while avoiding bulk alloying changes.
